# Atrial fibrillation

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Cardiology and angiology > Arrhythmias > Atrial fibrillation*

[Original Article Link](/library/GS0Baf)

---

## Summary

Atrial fibrillation (Afib) is a common type of <u>supraventricular tachyarrhythmia</u> characterized by uncoordinated atrial activation that results in an irregular ventricular response. <u>Afib with rapid ventricular response</u> (RVR) is Afib with a ventricular rate > 100–110/minute. While the exact mechanisms of Afib are poorly understood, associations with a number of cardiac (e.g., <u>valvular heart disease</u>, <u>coronary artery disease</u>) and noncardiac (e.g., <u>hyperthyroidism</u>, <u>electrolyte</u> imbalances) <u>risk factors</u> have been established. Individuals with Afib are typically asymptomatic. When symptoms do occur, they usually include <u>palpitations</u>, <u>lightheadedness</u>, and <u>shortness of breath</u>. <u>Physical examination</u> typically reveals an <u>irregularly irregular pulse</u>. Ineffective atrial emptying as a result of Afib can lead to stagnation of blood and clot formation in the <u>atria</u>, which in turn increases the risk of <u>stroke</u> and other thromboembolic complications. Diagnosis is confirmed with <u>ECG</u> showing absent <u>P waves</u> with irregular QRS intervals. <u>Echocardiography</u> is used to rule out <u>structural heart disease</u> and to evaluate for any atrial <u>thrombi</u>. Immediate <u>synchronized cardioversion</u> is required in <u>hemodynamically unstable</u> patients. In stable patients, treatment involves the correction of <u>modifiable risk factors</u>, rate or <u>rhythm control strategies</u>, and anticoagulation. Rate-control therapy typically involves the use of <u>beta blockers</u> or <u>nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers</u>. <u>Rhythm control strategies</u> include <u>synchronized electrical cardioversion</u>, the use of pharmacological <u>antiarrhythmics</u> (e.g., <u>flecainide</u>, <u>propafenone</u>, or <u>amiodarone</u>), and <u>ablation</u> of the arrhythmogenic tissue. Patients are typically started on anticoagulation depending on their <u>thrombotic</u> and bleeding risk.




<u>Atrial flutter</u> is another common type of <u>supraventricular tachyarrhythmia</u> that is usually caused by a single macroreentrant rhythm within the <u>atria</u>. The <u>risk factors</u> for <u>atrial flutter</u> are similar to those of Afib. In <u>atrial flutter</u>, the <u>ventricular rhythm</u> is usually regular. Treatment is also similar to that of Afib, consisting of anticoagulation and strategies to control <u>heart rate</u> and rhythm. <u>Atrial flutter</u> is typically more responsive to <u>ablation therapy</u> than Afib. <u>Atrial flutter</u> frequently progresses to Afib.

---

## Epidemiology

* Most common sustained <u>arrhythmia</u> [[1]](/library/ObWIFP0)

* <u>Incidence</u>: increases with age [[1]](/library/ObWIFP0)

* The lifetime risk of Afib among individuals > 40 years is 1 in 4.

* > 95% of individuals with Afib are ≥ 60 years

* <u>Prevalence</u>: approx. 1–2% of US population [[2]](/library/lbWvFP0)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

The exact <u>causes of atrial fibrillation</u> are unknown, but several <u>risk factors</u> have been identified (see table below).




### <u>Risk factors</u> [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)[[4]](/library/r-0fAi)[[5]](/library/U30b3f)




| Risk factors for atrial fibrillation |  |
| --- | --- |
| <u>Cardiovascular risk factors</u> | <br><br>* Advanced age<br><br>* <u>Hypertension</u><br><br>* <u>Diabetes mellitus</u><br><br>* Smoking<br><br>* <u>Obesity</u><br><br>* <u>Obstructive sleep apnea</u> (<u>OSA</u>)<br><br><br> |
| Intrinsic cardiac disorders | <br><br>* <u>Coronary artery disease</u> (<u>CAD</u>)<br><br>* <u>Valvular heart disease</u> (especially <u>mitral valve</u> disease)<br><br>* <u>Heart failure</u><br><br>* Preexcitation <u>tachycardia</u>. e.g., <u>Wolff-Parkinson-White</u> (<u>WPW</u>) syndrome<br><br>* <u>Sick sinus syndrome</u> (<u>tachycardia-bradycardia</u> syndrome)<br><br>* <u>Cardiomyopathies</u><br><br>* <u>Pericarditis</u><br><br>* Genetic predisposition (e.g., congenital channelopathies)<br><br>* <u>Atrial myxoma</u><br><br><br> |
| Noncardiac disorders | <br><br>* Pulmonary disease: <u>COPD</u>, <u>pulmonary embolism</u>, <u>pneumonia</u><br><br>* <u>Hyperthyroidism</u><br><br>* <u>Catecholamine</u> release and/or increased <u>sympathetic</u> activity<br><br>* <u>Stress</u>: <u>sepsis</u>, <u>hypovolemia</u>, post-surgical state (especially following cardiac <u>surgery</u>), <u>hypothermia</u><br><br>* <u>Pheochromocytoma</u><br><br>* <u>Cocaine</u>, <u>amphetamines</u><br><br>* <u>Electrolyte</u> imbalances (<u>hypomagnesemia</u>, <u>hypokalemia</u>)<br><br>* Drugs: e.g., <u>adenosine</u>, <u>digoxin</u><br><br>* Holiday heart syndrome: <u>irregular heartbeat</u> classically triggered by <u>excessive alcohol consumption</u>, but also sometimes by <u>moderate alcohol consumption</u>, <u>stress</u>, <u>dehydration</u>, or <u>lack of sleep</u><br><br>* <u>Chronic kidney disease</u>  [[6]](/library/BFbz4v)<br><br><br> |





### Reversible causes of atrial fibrillation [[7]](/library/ORXIMB)




* <u>Hyperthyroidism</u>, <u>thyrotoxicosis</u>

* <u>Electrolyte</u> imbalances

* Cardiothoracic <u>surgery</u>

* <u>Myocarditis</u>

* <u>Pericarditis</u>

* <u>Myocardial infarction</u>

* <u>Alcohol</u> use

* Excess <u>caffeine</u>

* <u>Fever</u> of any cause

* Recreational or pharmacological drug use

* <u>Pulmonary embolism</u>

* Other triggers of <u>tachycardia</u>: e.g., <u>pain</u>, <u>hypovolemia</u>, <u>anemia</u>





> [!NOTE]
> Approx. 15% of individuals who develop Afib have none of the above mentioned <u>risk factors</u> (<u>idiopathic</u>/lone Afib).




> [!NOTE]
> Remember PARASITE to memorize the major <u>risk factors</u> for acute Afib: P – Pulmonary disease; A – Anemia; R – Rheumatic <u>heart</u> disease; A – Atrial <u>myxoma</u>; S – Sepsis; I – Ischemia; T – Thyroid disease; E – Ethanol.

## Classification

### American College of Cardiology/American <u>Heart</u> Association (<u>ACC</u>/<u>AHA</u>) stages [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)




| <br>ACC/AHA stages of atrial fibrillation [[3]](/library/z6drnI0) |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stage |  | Definition and criteria |
| Stage 1: at risk for Afib |  | <br>* Certain <u>risk factors for Afib</u>, i.e.:<br><br>* Nonmodifiable: advanced age, male sex, and/or genetic predisposition<br><br>* Modifiable: <u>obesity</u>, lack of fitness, <u>hypertension</u>, <u>OSA</u>, <u>alcohol</u> consumption, and/or <u>diabetes mellitus</u><br><br> |
| Stage 2: pre-Afib |  | <br>* Further predisposition to Afib, i.e.:<br><br>* Comorbid conditions: <u>heart failure</u>, <u>CAD</u>, <u>hypertrophic cardiomyopathy</u> (<u>HCM</u>), neuromuscular disorders, and/or <u>thyroid disorders</u><br><br>* Structural or electrical abnormalities: atrial enlargement, frequent ectopy, brief <u>atrial tachycardia</u>, and/or <u>atrial flutter</u><br><br> |
| <br>Stage 3: Afib <br> | 3a: paroxysmal Afib | <br><br>* Afib that resolves within 7 days of onset either following treatment or spontaneously<br><br>* The frequency of recurring episodes may vary.<br><br><br> |
| 3b: persistent Afib | <br>* Continuous Afib for > 7 days<br><br> |  |
| 3c: long-standing persistent Afib | <br>* Continuous Afib for > 1 year<br><br> |  |
| 3d: successful Afib <u>ablation</u> | <br>* Afib that resolves after percutaneous or surgical intervention<br><br> |  |
| Stage 4: permanent Afib |  | <br>* Afib in which therapeutic attempts are no longer made to convert to or maintain <u>sinus rhythm</u>, unless the patient and the treating physician agree to do so<br><br> |

---

## Pathophysiology

* Atrial fibrillation is a <u>supraventricular arrhythmia</u>.

* The exact mechanisms of Afib are not well understood. Suggested mechanisms include:

* <u>Volume overload</u>, hemodynamic <u>stress</u> → atrial <u>hypertrophy</u> and/or dilatation

* Atrial <u>ischemia</u>

* Inflammation of the atrial <u>myocardium</u>

* Altered ion conduction by the atrial <u>myocardium</u>

* The new onset of Afib triggers a vicious circle that can ultimately lead to chronic Afib with atrial remodeling:
1. * Afib is triggered by one or both of the following

* Bursts of electrical activity from automatic foci near the <u>pulmonary vein</u> ostia (<u>left atrium</u>) or in diseased, <u>fibrotic</u> atrial tissue

* Pre-excitation of the <u>atria</u> as a result of aberrant pathways (e.g., <u>WPW syndrome</u>)
2. * Afib is sustained by re-entry rhythms and/or rapid focal <u>ectopic</u> firing 
* Re-entry rhythms are more likely to occur with enlarged <u>atria</u>, diseased <u>heart</u> tissue, and/or aberrant pathways (e.g., <u>WPW syndrome</u>).
3. * Atrial remodeling

* Electrophysiological changes in the <u>atria</u> occur within a few hours of Afib onset (electrical modeling).

* If Afib persists, atrial <u>fibrosis</u> and dilatation (structural remodeling) occur within a few months.

* Electrical and structural remodeling increase susceptibility to Afib, resulting in a vicious circle.

* Effects of Afib

* The <u>atria</u> contract rapidly but ineffectively and in an uncoordinated fashion → stasis of blood within the <u>atria</u> → risk of <u>thromboembolism</u> and <u>stroke</u>

* Irregular activation of the ventricles by conduction through the <u>AV node</u> → <u>tachycardia</u>

## Clinical features

* All patients

* <u>Irregularly irregular pulse</u>;  with or without <u>tachycardia</u>

* <u>Apex-pulse deficit</u>

* Stable Afib: Afib without signs of <u>hemodynamic instability</u>

* Most affected individuals are asymptomatic.

* Some may present with:

* <u>Palpitations</u>

* Fatigue

* <u>Dyspnea</u>

* <u>Lightheadedness</u>

* <u>Syncope</u>

* Signs of underlying <u>heart</u> disease (e.g., <u>murmurs</u> of <u>mitral stenosis</u>)

* Unstable Afib: Afib manifesting with signs of <u>hemodynamic instability</u>

* <u>Ischemic</u> <u>chest pain</u>

* <u>Altered mental status</u>

* <u>Clinical features of pulmonary edema</u>

* <u>Clinical features of acute heart failure</u>

* Clinical features of <u>cardiogenic shock</u>

* Complications of Afib

* Acute left <u>heart failure</u> → <u>pulmonary edema</u>

* <u>Thromboembolic events</u>: <u>stroke</u>/<u>TIA</u>, <u>renal infarct</u>, <u>splenic infarct</u> , <u>intestinal ischemia</u> , <u>acute limb ischemia</u>

* <u>Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Unstable Afib</u> is more likely to occur in patients with <u>Afib with RVR</u> and/or underlying cardiopulmonary disease.




> [!NOTE]
> Individuals with Afib may be asymptomatic for a long time before a diagnosis is made.




> [!NOTE]
> The <u>brain</u>, <u>kidney</u>, and <u>spleen</u> are the three organs most likely to be damaged by <u>emboli</u>!

---

## Diagnostics

### Diagnostic confirmation




#### Modalities




* 12-lead <u>ECG</u>: initial investigative study to confirm Afib

* Cardiac rhythm monitoring [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)

* Indications

* Suspected <u>paroxysmal Afib</u> if <u>ECG</u> is not diagnostic and clinical suspicion is high

* Evaluation of the adequacy of rate or <u>rhythm control</u> measures, and/or the presence of additional <u>arrhythmias</u> (e.g., <u>atrial flutter</u>)

* Assessment of the relationship between symptoms and Afib (patient-activated <u>event recorders</u>)

* Options

* <u>Ambulatory ECG monitoring</u>: <u>Holter monitor</u>, <u>event recorders</u>, <u>loop recorders</u>

* Inpatient: <u>continuous cardiac telemetry</u>





#### Findings




* Clinical Afib

* An episode of Afib documented on <u>ECG</u> lasting ≥ 30 seconds

* May be symptomatic or asymptomatic

* Subclinical Afib

* Asymptomatic Afib not detected on 12-lead <u>ECG</u>

* Detected on implanted cardiac devices and confirmed with <u>intracardiac electrography</u>  [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)[[12]](/library/8GbOav)

* Signs of comorbid conditions and/or underlying etiologies

* <u>Aberrant conduction</u>: e.g., <u>LBBB</u>, <u>RBBB</u>, <u>ECG findings in WPW</u>

* <u>CAD</u>: e.g., rate-dependent <u>ST depressions</u>, <u>ECG findings in STEMI</u>, <u>ECG findings of NSTE-ACS</u>, or evidence of previous <u>myocardial infarction</u>

* Others: e.g., <u>ECG findings in pericarditis</u>, <u>ECG signs of LVH</u>





| <br>ECG findings in atrial fibrillation [[13]](/library/1ib2qt)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | Appearance |
| Rhythm |  | <br><br>* <u>Irregularly irregular RR intervals</u><br><br>* Rarely may be regular if there is complete <u>AV dissociation</u><br><br><br> |
| Rate | Afib with RVR | <br>* Ventricular rate > 100–110/minute (<u>tachycardic</u> Afib)  [[14]](/library/2FYThI)[[15]](/library/rwbf4D)<br><br> |
| Afib with SVR (<u>slow Afib</u>) | <br>* Ventricular rate < 60/minute (<u>bradycardic</u> Afib or <u>slow Afib</u>)  [[16]](/library/mRbVnt)<br><br> |  |
| <u>P waves</u> |  | <br><br>* <u>P waves</u> are indiscernible.<br><br>* <u>Fibrillatory waves</u> (f waves) are seen instead at a frequency of 300–600/minute <br><br>* Recent-onset Afib: prominent, coarse f waves with higher amplitude in leads V<sub>1</sub>, II, III, and <u>aVF</u><br><br>* Chronic Afib: f waves have low <u>amplitudes</u> and may appear as an undulating baseline.<br><br>* <u>PR intervals</u>: not distinguishable<br><br><br> |
| <u>QRS complex</u> |  | <br><br>* Typically <u>narrow QRS complex</u> (< 0.12 seconds)<br><br>* <u>Wide QRS complex</u> may be seen in some situations:<br><br>* <u>Aberrant conduction</u>, e.g., <u>bundle branch block</u> or preexcitation (as seen in <u>Afib with WPW</u>)<br><br>* Complete <u>AV block</u> with a <u>ventricular escape rhythm</u><br><br>* Ashman phenomenon: intermittent aberrant ventricular conduction results in isolated or short runs of <u>wide QRS complexes</u><br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> Irregularly irregular <u>NCT</u> with a rate > 100–110/minute and no discernable <u>P waves</u> on <u>ECG</u> strongly suggests <u>Afib with RVR</u>.




> [!TIP]
> Regular <u>NCT</u> with a rate of 150/minute with sawtooth <u>P waves</u> on <u>ECG</u> suggests rapid <u>atrial flutter</u> with 2:1 conduction.




> [!TIP]
> RVR > 200/minute suggests <u>preexcited Afib</u> (usually with <u>wide QRS</u>) or an alternative diagnosis (e.g., VT).

### Routine studies




#### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)[[17]](/library/HRbKot)[[18]](/library/sjbtbF)




* <u>CBC</u>: assessment for <u>anemia</u> and signs of infection

* Serum <u>electrolytes</u> (Na<sup>+</sup>, <u>K<sup>+</sup></u>, <u>Mg<sup>2+</sup></u>, and <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u>): to identify <u>electrolyte</u> imbalances

* <u>BUN</u>, serum <u>creatinine</u>, and <u>liver chemistries</u>: to identify abnormal renal or <u>liver function</u>  [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)[[6]](/library/BFbz4v)[[19]](/library/BjbzcF)

* <u>TFTs</u>: to screen for <u>thyrotoxicosis</u>





> [!TIP]
> Avoid routine testing for <u>myocardial</u> <u>ischemia</u>, <u>ACS</u>, or <u>PE</u> if only Afib is present and there is no clinical suspicion for these conditions. [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)




> [!WARNING]
> Afib can independently cause elevated <u>D-dimer</u>, <u>troponin</u>, and <u>BNP</u> levels. Interpret these findings along with the overall clinical suspicion for underlying <u>PE</u>, <u>ACS</u>, and/or <u>CHF</u>. [[20]](/library/gx0FDR)[[21]](/library/WAbPiw)[[22]](/library/vA1Alj0)[[23]](/library/DA11Nj0)




#### <u>TTE</u> [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)[[24]](/library/LibwHt)




* Goal: to assess cardiac function and rule out underlying <u>structural heart disease</u> (e.g., <u>mitral valve stenosis</u>)

* Indications

* New <u>Afib diagnosis</u>

* Known Afib with clinical deterioration of unclear etiology

* Morphological <u>TTE</u> findings may include: [[24]](/library/LibwHt)[[25]](/library/dAboiw)[[26]](/library/oib0st)[[27]](/library/SPbyVF)

* Structurally normal <u>heart</u> (more common in young people)

* Left atrial <u>thrombus</u>

* Moderate to severe <u>mitral stenosis</u> or presence of a mechanical <u>heart valve</u> (previously known as valvular Afib) is associated with a significantly increased risk of <u>thromboembolic events</u>.  [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)[[28]](/library/kuYmrI)[[29]](/library/ibWJtP0)

* Other <u>valvular heart disease</u> or no valvulopathy (previously known as nonvalvular Afib)

* Atrial enlargement

* Functional <u>TTE</u> findings [[24]](/library/LibwHt)[[25]](/library/dAboiw)[[26]](/library/oib0st)[[27]](/library/SPbyVF)

* Chaotic atrial movements that are not coordinated with ventricles

* Decreased left atrial compliance and volume

* Decreased <u>LVEF</u> (due to <u>cardiomyopathy</u>)





> [!TIP]
> Patients with Afib should always be evaluated for mitral <u>valve dysfunction</u>.




### Additional studies




#### TEE for Afib [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)[[12]](/library/8GbOav)[[20]](/library/gx0FDR)[[30]](/library/iPbJeF)




* Goals

* To evaluate for <u>thrombi</u> and reduce the risk of <u>thromboembolic events</u> prior to <u>cardioversion</u>

* Visualize the <u>atria</u> and the <u>left atrial appendage</u> (hotspots for thrombogenesis)

* Indications  [[20]](/library/gx0FDR)[[30]](/library/iPbJeF); 

* New-onset Afib or <u>atrial flutter</u> of ≥ 48 hours or unknown duration

* No previous <u>anticoagulant</u> use or subtherapeutic anticoagulation

* High <u>stroke</u> risk (e.g., history of <u>stroke</u>, left atrial <u>thrombus</u>, <u>HOCM</u>, or <u>rheumatic fever</u>)

* Assessment of intracardiac <u>thrombus</u> resolution for <u>cardioversion</u>  [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)

* Findings of concern

* <u>Thrombus</u> in the <u>left atrium</u>, <u>left atrial appendage</u>, and/or <u>left ventricle</u>

* <u>Left atrial appendage</u> “smoke” and/or “sludge”

* Low <u>left atrial appendage</u> velocities

* Aortic <u>atheroma</u>  [[31]](/library/GBbBXw)

* Interpretation 

* No <u>thrombus</u> identified: Safe to proceed with <u>rhythm control</u>

* <u>Thrombus</u> identified: Anticoagulate for ≥ 3 weeks and consider repeat <u>TEE</u> prior to attempting <u>rhythm control</u>.





> [!TIP]
> <u>TEE</u> is performed prior to <u>cardioversion</u> to determine the safety of <u>rhythm control</u> in patients at risk of <u>thromboemboli</u> (e.g., Afib onset ≥ 48 hours) who cannot wait for ≥ 3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation.




![Thrombus in the left atrial appendage](media/v2x2jn055pwpch70tbly8r0k.jpg)

Thrombus in the left atrial appendage




#### Chest imaging [[20]](/library/gx0FDR)




* Goal: to evaluate for underlying cardiopulmonary comorbidities or etiologies

* <u>CXR</u>: e.g., <u>CXR findings of AHF</u>, <u>CXR findings of pneumonia</u>, <u>CXR findings of COPD</u>

* <u>CT pulmonary angiography</u>: See “Findings” in “<u>CTPA</u>.”





![Hydrostatic pulmonary edema](media/ginc5vuds0e3t20sd26axo4c.jpg)

Hydrostatic pulmonary edema

![Pulmonary embolism](media/y2ujb19xkxzzzwxdgumvf872.jpg)

Pulmonary embolism




#### Specialized testing [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)




Consider in patients with unexplained and early-onset Afib.




* <u>Electrophysiology study</u> (<u>EP study</u>) in patients < 30 years of age in order to: [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)[[20]](/library/gx0FDR)

* Identify associated conduction abnormalities (e.g., preexcitation)

* Identify lesions amenable to <u>ablation</u> (e.g., for <u>pulmonary vein isolation</u>)

* Distinguish between <u>ventricular tachycardia</u> and Afib with <u>aberrant conduction</u>

* In patients < 45 years of age, consider referral for <u>genetic counseling</u>, <u>genetic testing</u> for rare pathogenic variants, and monitoring for <u>cardiomyopathy</u>. [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)





### Testing for reversible <u>causes of Afib</u> or triggers




Consider additional studies based on clinical suspicion to evaluate for:




* Underlying etiologies: e.g., <u>sepsis workup</u>, <u>ACS diagnostics</u>, <u>PE diagnostics</u>, <u>CXR</u>, toxicology screen

* Comorbidities: e.g., <u>diabetes screening</u>, <u>CAD diagnostics</u>

* Complications: e.g., <u>ischemic stroke diagnostics</u>, <u>AHF diagnostics</u>

---

## Differential diagnoses

* <u>Tachycardia</u>

* See “<u>Differential diagnosis of irregular, narrow-complex tachycardia</u>.”

* See “<u>Differential diagnosis of SVT</u>.”

* See “<u>Differential diagnosis of wide-complex tachycardia</u>.”

* <u>Palpitations</u> [[32]](/library/Y4bn3F)

* <u>Cardiac arrhythmias</u>

* <u>Valvular heart disease</u> (e.g., <u>aortic stenosis</u> or <u>regurgitation</u>, <u>mitral valve prolapse</u>)

* <u>Cardiomyopathy</u>

* <u>Hyperthyroidism</u>

* <u>Hypoglycemia</u>

* <u>Hypovolemia</u>

* Drugs (e.g., <u>alcohol</u>, <u>cocaine</u>, <u>caffeine</u>)

* Psychiatric disorders (e.g., <u>panic attack</u>, <u>anxiety</u>)

* Other symptoms

* See also “<u>Syncope</u>.”

* See also “<u>Chest pain</u>.”

* See also “<u>Dyspnea</u>.”





> [!WARNING]
> Differentiate Afib from other <u>narrow complex tachycardias</u>, e.g., <u>SVT</u>, <u>multifocal AT</u>, <u>focal AT</u> with variable conduction, and <u>atrial flutter with variable conduction</u>.




> [!WARNING]
> Irregularly irregular <u>wide complex tachycardia</u> may represent Afib with <u>aberrant conduction</u>, <u>preexcited Afib</u>, or <u>ventricular tachycardia</u>. If in doubt, treat it as <u>ventricular tachycardia</u>.




![Tachycardia differentials](media/ot3278dk55q6ryh4vqa47yp2.jpg)

Tachycardia differentials




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Management

If the diagnosis is uncertain, see “<u>Management of unstable tachycardia with pulse</u>” or “<u>Management of stable, regular narrow-complex tachycardia</u>.”




### Approach




* Evaluate hemodynamic stability using the <u>ABCDE approach</u>.

* <u>Establish IV access</u>.

* Begin <u>continuous cardiac monitoring</u> and <u>pulse oximetry</u>.

* Obtain confirmatory 12-lead <u>ECG</u> and other <u>Afib diagnostics</u>.

* Identify and treat reversible <u>causes of Afib</u>.

* Consider comorbid conditions that affect management; see:

* “<u>Management of Afib with ACS</u>”

* “Management of Afib with chronic HF”

* “<u>Management of preexcited Afib</u>”





> [!WARNING]
> Conduct a careful clinical evaluation to determine whether <u>tachycardia</u> is the primary cause of <u>hemodynamic instability</u> or a response to <u>shock</u> due to an underlying condition (e.g., <u>sepsis</u>, <u>hypovolemia</u>, <u>massive PE</u>), especially in patients with chronic Afib. [[33]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




> [!TIP]
> Patients with Afib detected during an acute medical condition (e.g., <u>sepsis</u>) or <u>surgery</u> are at high risk of Afib recurrence after recovery; consider outpatient follow-up for surveillance and assessment of thromboembolic risk. [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)




![Management of newly diagnosed atrial fibrillation](media/gneff3vc3tatns3yh95as40l.jpg)

Management of newly diagnosed atrial fibrillation




### Unstable Afib management [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)




* Manage <u>unstable Afib</u> with immediate <u>synchronized electrical cardioversion</u>. [[34]](/library/HnXKuA)

* <u>Afib with RVR</u>: 120–200 J biphasic

* <u>Atrial flutter</u> with RVR: 50–100 J biphasic

* Anticoagulate as soon as possible if indicated, but do not delay emergency <u>electrical cardioversion</u> for preprocedural anticoagulation.





### <u>Stable Afib</u> [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)




* Consider acute pharmacological <u>rate control for Afib</u> with RVR to improve symptoms.

* Consider long-term <u>rhythm vs. rate control</u> based on:

* Need for <u>pericardioversion anticoagulation for Afib</u> (e.g., onset ≥ 48 hours or unknown)

* <u>Shared decision-making</u> and additional individual factors (see “<u>Rhythm vs. rate control</u>”)

* Begin <u>long-term anticoagulation for Afib</u> if favored by risk assessment, i.e.:

* <u>Thrombotic</u> complications: e.g., <u>CHA<sub>2</sub>DS<sub>2</sub>-VASc score</u>, <u>TEE for Afib</u>

* Risk of bleeding: e.g., <u>coagulation studies</u>, <u>HAS-BLED score</u>





#### Ottawa aggressive protocol  [[35]](/library/iCYJ7r)[[36]](/library/QCYu7r)




* A protocol for <u>rhythm control</u> in the ED for eligible patients < 48 hours from Afib onset followed by discharge after a 1-hour observation and rapid cardiology follow-up

* Involves <u>pharmacological cardioversion</u> using <u>procainamide</u> DOSAGE and, if unsuccessful, <u>synchronized electrical cardioversion</u> at 150–200 J (biphasic)





### Acute decompensation




Patients with known Afib may seek care for acutely decompensated or recurrent Afib and/or comorbid conditions complicated by Afib (e.g., <u>heart failure</u>, <u>ACS</u>, <u>sepsis</u>).




* For unstable patients, see “<u>Unstable Afib management</u>.”

* For all other stable patients:

* Assess adherence to therapy (e.g., <u>rate control</u> medications, <u>anticoagulation for Afib</u>).

* Identify and manage <u>reversible Afib triggers</u>.

* Evaluate for and address conditions that could alter treatment <u>efficacy</u> (e.g., new-onset <u>AKI</u>, medication interactions).

* Follow any existing treatment plan for <u>rate control</u> or <u>rhythm control</u>.

* Consult the patient's treating cardiologist as needed.

* Manage complications and comorbid conditions on an individual basis.





### Supportive management




* <u>Immediate hemodynamic support</u> with judicious <u>IV fluids</u> and cautious use of <u>vasopressors</u>

* Consider <u>procedural sedation for cardioversion</u>.

* Begin <u>pericardioversion anticoagulation for Afib</u> as soon as possible if Afib onset is ≥ 48 hours or unknown and the patient is not already anticoagulated.





### Disposition [[33]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* Patients presenting to the ED typically undergo a trial of <u>rate control</u> or <u>rhythm control</u> followed by a period of observation.

* Hospital admission is required for symptomatic patients unresponsive to ED management.

* Consider cardiology consult and <u>ICU</u> admission for patients with persistently unstable or refractory <u>tachycardia</u>.

* Consider discharge with close outpatient cardiology follow-up in stable, asymptomatic patients with:

* Resolved RVR or successful <u>cardioversion</u>

* AND underlying <u>reversible Afib trigger</u> that has been adequately treated

* Follow local protocols and consider cardiology consultation prior to discharge.  [[37]](/library/bZWHZP0)

* For inpatients who develop new Afib or experience recurrence or decompensation, consult cardiology.





### Follow-up care




The following measures can be applied in inpatient or outpatient settings.




* Optimize long-term therapy for chronic underlying <u>Afib etiologies</u> and related comorbidities.

* Manage <u>cardiovascular risk factors</u> and encourage lifestyle modifications (e.g., weight loss, exercise, <u>OSA management</u>, reduction of <u>alcohol</u> consumption).  [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)[[12]](/library/8GbOav)[[28]](/library/kuYmrI)

* Monitor <u>kidney</u> and <u>liver function</u> regularly for patients on anticoagulation. [[28]](/library/kuYmrI)

* Educate patients on <u>treatment adherence</u>, risk of <u>thromboembolism</u>, and risks of anticoagulation and/or <u>antiarrhythmic drugs</u>.

* Monitor for adverse effects of long-term treatment (e.g., <u>adverse effects of amiodarone</u>). [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)

---

## Rate control vs. rhythm control

### Overview




* There are no specific indications for <u>rate control</u> or <u>rhythm control</u>.

* Early <u>rhythm control</u> (i.e., within one year of diagnosis) is associated with a decreased risk of cardiovascular events  in all patients with Afib. [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)[[38]](/library/hr1cSR0)

* The choice of strategy is typically guided by:

* Afib characteristics (e.g., Afib stage, previous therapy, symptoms)

* Individual <u>risk factors</u> and comorbidities

* <u>Shared decision-making</u>

* Consultation with a specialist (e.g., a cardiologist or electrophysiologist) is strongly recommended.





| <br>Rate control vs. rhythm control [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)[[39]](/library/KxYUxr)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | <u>Rhythm control</u> | <u>Rate control</u> |
| Goals |  | <br><br>* Termination of Afib (or <u>atrial flutter</u>)<br><br>* Restoration and maintenance of <u>sinus rhythm</u><br><br>* Improvement of symptoms<br><br>* Prevention of atrial remodeling<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Decreased ventricular response rate to improve symptoms (in both acute and chronic Afib)<br><br>* Decreased risk of <u>arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Potential indications [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)<br> |  | <br><br>* Age < 70 years  [[40]](/library/4_13oj0)<br><br>* Highly symptomatic<br><br>* Recent-onset Afib (< 12 months)<br><br>* Failure of prior <u>rate control strategy</u> to control symptoms or achieve target <u>heart rate</u><br><br>* <u>TTE</u> findings (e.g., small <u>left atrium</u>, AV <u>regurgitation</u>, <u>LV dysfunction</u>)<br><br>* Treated reversible cause of Afib<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Age ≥ 70 years  [[40]](/library/4_13oj0)<br><br>* Milder symptoms<br><br>* Recurrent or <u>long-standing persistent Afib</u>  [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)[[41]](/library/j_1_Lj0)<br><br>* <u>Heart rate</u> is easily controlled.<br><br>* <u>TTE</u> findings (e.g., large <u>left atrium</u>, no or mild AV <u>regurgitation</u>, no or mild <u>LV dysfunction</u>)<br><br>* Untreated reversible cause of Afib<br><br>* High risk of <u>thromboembolism</u><br><br>* High risk of <u>adverse reactions</u> to <u>cardioversion</u><br><br><br> |
| Treatment modalities |  | <br><br>* <u>Cardioversion</u><br><br>* Emergency <u>synchronized cardioversion</u> (for <u>management of unstable Afib</u>)<br><br>* Planned <u>electrical cardioversion</u><br><br>* <u>Pharmacological cardioversion</u><br><br>* Long-term <u>maintenance therapy</u><br><br>* <u>Antiarrhythmic drug</u> therapy<br><br>* Afib <u>catheter ablation</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Acute pharmacological <u>rate control</u><br><br>* Long-term pharmacological <u>rate control</u><br><br>* <u>Atrioventricular node ablation</u><br><br><br> |





> [!WARNING]
> All types of <u>cardioversion</u> (electrical, pharmacological) can precipitate <u>arterial thromboembolism</u> and <u>stroke</u> in at-risk patients with Afib.




> [!WARNING]
> Evaluate the need for <u>pericardioversion anticoagulation for Afib</u> and consider delaying <u>cardioversion</u> until <u>TEE for Afib</u> has ruled out <u>thrombi</u> in patients at high risk.

---

## Rate control

### General principles




* <u>Rate control</u> in acute and chronic Afib is indicated for symptom control and to prevent <u>LV dysfunction</u>.

* Target <u>resting heart rate</u>

* < 100–110/minute: in patients without <u>heart failure</u> whose symptoms are well controlled at this rate

* < 80/minute in patients with either:

* <u>Heart failure</u>

* Persistence of symptoms at higher <u>heart rates</u>





> [!TIP]
> In patients with normal LV systolic function, outcomes with a lenient <u>rate control</u> of < 110/minute are similar to outcomes with a strict <u>rate control</u> of < 80/minute. [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)[[42]](/library/kNbmY8)




### Acute pharmacological <u>rate control</u>




* Patients without <u>decompensated HF</u>

* First-line

* <u>Beta blockers</u>, e.g.: <u>metoprolol</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[3]](/library/z6drnI0), <u>esmolol</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[3]](/library/z6drnI0), <u>propranolol</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)

* <u>ndHP CCBs</u>, e.g.: <u>diltiazem</u> DOSAGE [[3]](/library/z6drnI0), <u>verapamil</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)

* Second-line: if refractory or contraindications to first-line agents

* <u>Digoxin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[3]](/library/z6drnI0) (use with caution in older patients)  [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)

* <u>Amiodarone</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE  [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)

* Patients with <u>decompensated HF</u>: <u>amiodarone</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE  [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)

* All patients: Consider adding <u>magnesium</u> IV (<u>off-label</u>).

* Afib during <u>pregnancy</u> [[43]](/library/BdWzH40)[[44]](/library/ydWds40)

* <u>Beta blockers</u> are preferred.

* <u>CCBs</u> and <u>digoxin</u> can be used in consultation with a specialist.

* <u>Amiodarone</u> can lead to adverse fetal effects (e.g., neonatal <u>thyroid disorders</u>, <u>fetal growth restriction</u>) and should be avoided.





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>beta blockers</u> and <u>ndHP CCBs</u> in patients with <u>LV dysfunction</u> and <u>decompensated HF</u> as they can compromise hemodynamic function. [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)[[34]](/library/HnXKuA)




> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>AV nodal blockers</u> and <u>amiodarone</u> in patients with <u>preexcited Afib</u> as these can trigger <u>Vfib</u>. [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)




### Long-term pharmacological <u>rate control</u> [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)




* First-line

* <u>Beta blockers</u>: e.g., <u>metoprolol</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[3]](/library/z6drnI0), <u>atenolol</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[3]](/library/z6drnI0), <u>propranolol</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)

* Preferred for Afib during <u>pregnancy</u>

* Consider for Afib due to <u>hyperthyroidism</u>.

* Avoid in patients with <u>asthma</u>.

* OR nondihydropyridine <u>calcium channel blockers</u>: e.g., <u>diltiazem</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[3]](/library/z6drnI0), <u>verapamil</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)

* Contraindicated in patients with <u>LVEF</u> < 40%

* Can be safely used in <u>heart failure</u> with preserved normal LV systolic function

* Second-line: <u>digoxin</u> DOSAGE; preferred initial therapy for patients with <u>HFrEF</u> [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)

* Third-line: <u>amiodarone</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE; for patients who are critically ill and/or have <u>ADHF</u> and refractory Afib  [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)





### Atrioventricular node ablation [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)




* Indications 

* Recurrent Afib

* Afib refractory to pharmacological rate or <u>rhythm control strategies</u>

* Adverse effects to pharmacological rate or <u>rhythm control strategies</u>

* Procedure

* The <u>AV node</u> is destroyed during <u>cardiac catheterization</u> using high-frequency <u>radio</u> waves to cause a permanent <u>AV block</u>.

* Requires implantation of a permanent ventricular pacemaker (ideally 4–6 weeks prior)

---

## Rhythm control

### Cardioversion




#### Planned <u>electrical cardioversion</u> [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)[[12]](/library/8GbOav)




* Description

* Gradually increasing strengths of current (synchronized with the R wave) are administered under sedation until <u>sinus rhythm</u> is restored.

* The adjunctive use of <u>antiarrhythmic drugs</u> prior to <u>shock</u> delivery increases the likelihood of success.

* Indications

* Afib in hemodynamically stable patients who can tolerate sedation and prefer this option

* Unsuccessful <u>pharmacological cardioversion</u>





#### Pharmacological cardioversion  [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)[[34]](/library/HnXKuA)[[45]](/library/Bz1zEj0)




* Description: pharmacotherapy for the conversion of Afib to <u>sinus rhythm</u>

* Most likely to be effective for <u>arrhythmias</u> of < 7 days' duration [[20]](/library/gx0FDR)

* More effective for <u>atrial flutter</u> than Afib, but there is a risk of conversion to 1:1 conduction with <u>propafenone</u> and <u>flecainide</u>  [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)

* Indications

* Hemodynamically stable patients, in whom <u>procedural sedation</u> may be harmful

* Patient preference

* In-hospital setting (under <u>continuous cardiac monitoring</u>)

* Normal LV function: IV <u>amiodarone</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[3]](/library/z6drnI0) or <u>ibutilide</u>   DOSAGE; alternatively, <u>procainamide</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)

* <u>HFrEF</u>: IV <u>amiodarone</u>

* Pill-in-pocket strategy: a single, self-administered dose of an antiarrhythmic used outside of the hospital to terminate Afib

* Indication: infrequent, recent-onset Afib after a first successful dose in a hospital setting

* Agents: <u>flecainide</u>;  (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[3]](/library/z6drnI0) or <u>propafenone</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)

* Typically given in conjunction with a <u>beta blocker</u> or <u>ndHP CCB</u>





> [!TIP]
> If <u>pharmacological cardioversion</u> fails, avoid switching <u>antiarrhythmic drugs</u>; proceeding with planned <u>electrical cardioversion</u> is the recommended next step. [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)




> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>flecainide</u> and <u>propafenone</u> in patients with previous <u>myocardial infarction</u> and significant <u>structural heart disease</u>. [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)




### Pericardioversion anticoagulation for Afib [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)[[12]](/library/8GbOav)




Determine the need for pericardioversion anticoagulation based on the risk of <u>arterial thromboembolism</u> and considering the following:




* Duration of Afib

* Structural <u>heart</u> abnormalities: i.e., moderate to severe <u>mitral stenosis</u>, mechanical <u>heart valves</u>, or <u>HCM</u>

* <u>CHA<sub>2</sub>DS<sub>2</sub>-VASc</u> score





> [!WARNING]
> Patients with moderate to severe <u>mitral stenosis</u>, mechanical <u>heart valves</u>, or <u>HCM</u> are at high risk of <u>thromboembolism</u> regardless of duration since Afib onset or <u>CHA<sub>2</sub>DS<sub>2</sub>-VASc</u> score. If not already anticoagulated, consult cardiology for optimal pericardioversion management.




| <br><u>Pericardioversion anticoagulation for Afib</u> [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)[[12]](/library/8GbOav)[[28]](/library/kuYmrI)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | Before <u>cardioversion</u> | After <u>cardioversion</u> |
| Onset < 48 hours | <br>Low risk (<u>CHA<sub>2</sub>DS<sub>2</sub>-VASc</u> score 0 in men and 1 in women) <br> | <br>* Consider either:<br><br>* No anticoagulation<br><br>* Anticoagulation (with <u>heparin</u> or a <u>DOAC</u>) begun as soon as possible prior to the procedure<br><br> | <br>* Long-term anticoagulation is not routinely required.<br><br> |
| <br>Moderate risk (<u>CHA<sub>2</sub>DS<sub>2</sub>-VASc</u> score 1 in men and 2 in women) | <br>* Consider on an individual basis in consultation with cardiology.  [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)[[28]](/library/kuYmrI)<br><br> |  |  |
| <br><br>High risk  <u>CHA<sub>2</sub>DS<sub>2</sub>-VASc</u> score ≥ 2 in men and ≥ 3 in women)<br> | <br><br>* Anticoagulation with <u>heparin</u> or a <u>DOAC</u> begun as soon as possible prior to the procedure<br><br>* Precardioversion <u>TEE</u> may be considered to rule out intracardiac <u>thrombi</u>.<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Long-term anticoagulation for Afib</u> is usually indicated.<br><br> |  |
| Onset ≥ 48 hours or unknown | Stable patients | <br><br>* Anticoagulation with a <u>DOAC</u> or <u>warfarin</u> for 3 weeks prior to the procedure is preferred.<br><br>* In patients who cannot wait 3 weeks, a precardioversion <u>TEE</u> to rule out <u>thrombi</u> should be requested.<br><br><br> | <br>* At least 4 weeks of oral anticoagulation is preferred.<br><br> |
| Unstable patients | <br>* Begin anticoagulation with <u>heparin</u> or a <u>DOAC</u> as soon as possible without delaying emergency <u>electrical cardioversion</u>.<br><br> |  |  |





> [!TIP]
> Base decisions about postcardioversion <u>long-term anticoagulation for Afib</u> on individual <u>thrombotic</u> and bleeding risk profiles. [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)




![Anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation](media/h96i2307i6u1ikv4u5t22wfu.jpg)

Anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation




### Long-term rhythm maintenance [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)




#### Antiarrhythmic pharmacotherapy




* Indications: patients with recurrent Afib and low risk of adverse effects

* No <u>structural heart disease</u> and normal <u>LVEF</u>

* First-line agents: <u>dofetilide</u>, <u>dronedarone</u>, <u>flecainide</u>, and <u>propafenone</u>

* Second-line agents: <u>amiodarone</u> and <u>sotalol</u>

* <u>Structural heart disease</u> or <u>LVEF</u> ≤ 40%

* First-line agents: <u>amiodarone</u>, <u>dofetilide</u>  [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)

* Avoid <u>flecainide</u>, <u>sotalol</u>, and <u>propafenone</u>.





#### Afib <u>catheter ablation</u> [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)[[20]](/library/gx0FDR)




* Description: creation of <u>scar</u> tissue that prevents the spread of <u>ectopic</u> impulses

* Indications include:

* First-line for symptomatic <u>paroxysmal Afib</u> in younger patients with few comorbidities

* Symptomatic Afib refractory or with contraindications to <u>pharmacological cardioversion</u>

* Patients undergoing cardiac <u>surgery</u> unrelated to Afib

* Selected patients with concurrent <u>HFrEF</u> (e.g., younger patients without significant comorbidities, earlier <u>HF stages</u>)  [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)[[12]](/library/8GbOav)[[46]](/library/-NbDd8)

* Modalities

* Pulmonary vein isolation; : catheter <u>radiofrequency ablation</u> of atrial tissue around <u>pulmonary vein</u> openings  [[12]](/library/8GbOav)

* Maze ablation: A series of <u>incisions</u> are made in the atrial <u>endocardium</u> via a catheter or surgically to prevent atrial macroentry.

---

## Long-term anticoagulation

For patients with new-onset Afib being considered for <u>rhythm control</u>, see “<u>Pericardioversion anticoagulation in Afib</u>.”




### Approach




Use the same risk-benefit profile assessment for all <u>types of Afib</u> and <u>atrial flutter</u> (e.g., <u>paroxysmal Afib</u>, <u>persistent Afib</u>), treatment strategies (i.e., rate or <u>rhythm control</u>), or apparent maintenance of <u>sinus rhythm</u>. [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)[[12]](/library/8GbOav)




* Assess <u>thrombotic</u> risk.

* Identify patients at high risk of <u>thromboembolism</u> (i.e., those with moderate to severe <u>mitral stenosis</u>, mechanical <u>heart valves</u>, and <u>HCM</u>).

* Calculate <u>CHA<sub>2</sub>DS<sub>2</sub>-VASc</u> score in all other patients.

* Assess bleeding risk.

* Identify <u>contraindications to anticoagulation</u>.

* Calculate <u>HAS-BLED</u> score.

* Choose the appropriate <u>anticoagulation regimen for Afib</u> based on the individual risk profile.

* Consider interventional alternatives for patients with <u>contraindications to anticoagulation</u> and a high <u>thrombotic</u> risk.





> [!TIP]
> Prevention of <u>thromboembolism</u> with long-term anticoagulation is typically indicated in patients with moderate to severe <u>mitral stenosis</u>, mechanical <u>heart valves</u>, <u>HCM</u>, and/or a <u>CHA<sub>2</sub>DS<sub>2</sub>-VASc</u> score ≥ 2 in men and ≥ 3 in women.




> [!WARNING]
> Always consider the bleeding risk when initiating anticoagulation.




![Anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation](media/h96i2307i6u1ikv4u5t22wfu.jpg)

Anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation




### Risk assessment [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)




Evaluate <u>thrombotic</u> risk and bleeding risk for all patients with Afib and <u>atrial flutter</u> regardless of classification and treatment strategy.




| <u>Thrombotic</u> risk in Afib and <u>atrial flutter</u> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Conditions | Recommendation |
| High risk | <br><br>* Moderate to severe <u>mitral stenosis</u>, mechanical <u>heart valves</u>, or <u>HCM</u> [[47]](/library/BObzuF)<br><br>* All other patients: <u>CHA<sub>2</sub>DS<sub>2</sub>-VASc</u> score ≥ 2 in men or ≥ 3 in women<br><br><br> | <br>* Anticoagulation is recommended.<br><br> |
| Moderate risk | <br><br>* No moderate to severe <u>mitral stenosis</u>, mechanical <u>heart valves</u>, or <u>HCM</u><br><br>* <u>CHA<sub>2</sub>DS<sub>2</sub>-VASc</u> score of 1 in men or 2 in women<br><br><br> | <br>* Consider anticoagulation using <u>shared decision-making</u>.<br><br> |
| Low risk | <br><br>* No moderate to severe <u>mitral stenosis</u>, mechanical <u>heart valves</u>, or <u>HCM</u><br><br>* <u>CHA<sub>2</sub>DS<sub>2</sub>-VASc</u> score of 0 in men or 1 in women<br><br><br> | <br>* Anticoagulation is not routinely recommended.<br><br> |





> [!WARNING]
> Do not use <u>CHA<sub>2</sub>DS<sub>2</sub>-VASc</u> scores to risk <u>stratify</u> patients with moderate to severe <u>mitral stenosis</u>, mechanical <u>heart valves</u>, or <u>HCM</u>. [[28]](/library/kuYmrI)




#### CHA<sub>2</sub>DS<sub>2</sub>-VASc score




* A validated scoring system for assessing the risk of <u>stroke</u> in Afib  [[48]](/library/2kbTMF)

* Avoid use in patients with moderate to severe <u>mitral stenosis</u>, mechanical <u>heart valves</u>, or <u>HCM</u>. [[28]](/library/kuYmrI)





| <br><u>CHA<sub>2</sub>DS<sub>2</sub>-VASc score</u> [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)[[49]](/library/UkbbMF)[[50]](/library/TOb67F)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
| <u>Risk factor</u> | Points |
| <br><u>Congestive heart failure</u> or <u>LV dysfunction</u> <br> | 1 |
| <u>Hypertension</u> | 1 |
| Age ≥ 75 years | 2 |
| <u>Diabetes mellitus</u> | 1 |
| Prior <u>stroke</u>, <u>transient ischemic attack</u>, or <u>thromboembolism</u> | 2 |
| <br>Vascular disease <br> | 1 |
| Age 65–74 years | 1 |
| <br>Sex: female  [[48]](/library/2kbTMF)[[51]](/library/RJdlFI0)<br> | 1 |
| <br>Risk of <u>stroke</u>  [[52]](/library/fkbkMF) <br><br>* 0 points (male) or 0–1 point (female): low risk<br><br>* 1 point (male) or 2 points (female): intermediate risk<br><br>* ≥ 2 points (male) or ≥ 3 points (female): high risk<br><br><br><br> |  |





![CHADS2-VASc score](media/zg5q806cae9x5b9jeq72bma4.jpg)

CHADS2-VASc score




#### HAS-BLED score  [[53]](/library/gObF7F)




* Most often used to assess the risk of bleeding in patients starting anticoagulation.  [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)[[54]](/library/SOby7F)

* Consider addressing <u>modifiable risk factors</u>, e.g., uncontrolled <u>hypertension</u>, <u>alcohol</u> use, <u>NSAID</u>, or <u>aspirin</u> use, and reevaluating risk.

* A high-risk <u>HAS-BLED</u> score is not necessarily a reason to withhold anticoagulation; these patients require more frequent monitoring. [[50]](/library/TOb67F)





| <br><u>HAS-BLED score</u> [[53]](/library/gObF7F)[[54]](/library/SOby7F)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
| Characteristics | Points |
| <br>Uncontrolled <u>hypertension</u> <br> | 1 |
| Abnormal renal or <u>liver function</u> | 1 point each (max. 2) |
| <br><u>Stroke</u> <br> | 1 |
| Bleeding history or predisposition | 1 |
| <br>Labile <u>INR</u> <br> | 1 |
| Older individuals (age > 65) | 1 |
| <br>Drugs that predispose to bleeding  or <u>alcohol</u> use <br> | 1 point each (max. 2) |
| <br>Interpretation [[55]](/library/7xb4BD) <br><br>* 0 points: low risk<br><br>* 1–2 points: moderate risk<br><br>* ≥ 3: high risk<br><br><br><br> |  |





![HAS-BLED score: Bleeding risk in atrial fibrillation](media/rlvuqhrcp6rg4x3otcjwx6ot.jpg)

HAS-BLED score: Bleeding risk in atrial fibrillation




### Anticoagulation regimens in atrial fibrillation and <u>atrial flutter</u> [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)




The choice of <u>anticoagulant</u> is predominantly based on individual patient factors.




* Educate patients on <u>treatment adherence</u>, bleeding risk, and risk-mitigating behavior modifications.  [[56]](/library/HBbKXw)[[57]](/library/UzbbHw)

* <u>Antiplatelets</u> are no longer recommended as an alternative to anticoagulation for <u>stroke</u> prevention in Afib or <u>atrial flutter</u>. [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)[[12]](/library/8GbOav)

* See “<u>Pericardioversion anticoagulation in Afib</u>” for indications and agents for anticoagulation prior to <u>cardioversion</u> for <u>rhythm control</u>.





| <br>Long-term anticoagulation options in atrial fibrillation and flutter [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)[[18]](/library/sjbtbF)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Clinical applications | Options | Special considerations |
| <u>DOACs</u> | <br>* All patients without:<br><br>* Moderate to severe <u>mitral stenosis</u> or mechanical <u>heart valves</u><br><br>* Contraindications to <u>DOACs</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Dabigatran</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Rivaroxaban</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Apixaban</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Edoxaban</u> DOSAGE<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Avoid in <u>pregnancy</u>.<br><br>* May not be suitable in severe renal impairment<br><br>* Preferred for patients who cannot adhere to regular <u>INR</u> monitoring<br><br><br> |
| <u>Vitamin K antagonists</u> (<u>VKAs</u>) | <br><br>* Patients with moderate to severe <u>mitral stenosis</u> or mechanical <u>heart valves</u><br><br>* Patients with contraindications to <u>DOACs</u><br><br>* Patients with severe hepatic dysfunction<br><br>* Patients with advanced <u>CKD</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Warfarin</u> DOSAGE [[28]](/library/kuYmrI)[[58]](/library/HuYKsI)<br><br> | <br><br>* Avoid in <u>pregnancy</u>.<br><br>* <u>Bridging anticoagulation</u> may be indicated.<br><br>* Requires weekly <u>INR</u> measurement initially, followed by monthly <u>INR</u> measurements once therapeutic levels have been reached [[28]](/library/kuYmrI)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Heparin</u> | <br><br>* <u>Pregnancy</u><br><br>* <u>Periprocedural bridging anticoagulation</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Unfractionated heparin</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>LMWH</u> (e.g., <u>enoxaparin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE, <u>dalteparin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE) [[59]](/library/sBbtXw)<br><br><br> | <br>* Use <u>LMWH</u> with caution in renal impairment.<br><br> |





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>dabigatran</u> in patients with Afib and mechanical <u>heart valves</u> as it can be harmful. [[28]](/library/kuYmrI)




### Interventional alternatives to anticoagulation [[3]](/library/z6drnI0)




* Description: occlusion of the <u>left atrial appendage</u> (most common location for the <u>formation of thrombus</u>) [[60]](/library/2zbTHw)

* Options include

* Percutaneous <u>left atrial appendage</u> occlusion

* Surgical occlusion of the <u>left atrial appendage</u>

* Considered in patients who have <u>contraindications to anticoagulation</u> and an increased risk of <u>stroke</u>.  [[12]](/library/8GbOav)

## Atrial flutter

### Definition



* <u>Atrial flutter</u> is a <u>supraventricular tachyarrhythmia</u> that is usually caused by a macroreentrant rhythm within the <u>atria</u>. [[20]](/library/gx0FDR)




### <u>Epidemiology</u> [[67]](/library/9mbN38)




* <u>Incidence</u>: 88 per 100,000 <u>person-years</u> (increases with age)

* Sex: <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> (<u>incidence</u> in men is 2.5 times greater than in women)





### Etiology




* Similar to atrial fibrillation (see “Etiology” section above)

* May additionally result from the treatment of Afib  [[14]](/library/2FYThI)





### Pathophysiology




* Type I (common; ; typical or <u>isthmus</u>-dependent flutter): caused by a counterclockwise (more common) or clockwise (less common) macroreentrant activation of <u>cardiac muscle</u> fibers in the <u>right atrium</u> that travels along the tricuspid annulus and passes through the <u>cavotricuspid isthmus</u>

* Type II (rare; atypical <u>atrial flutter</u>): various reentrant rhythms;  that do not involve the cavotricuspid <u>isthmus</u>, are not well-defined, are usually around the tricuspid annulus, and/or occur in the <u>left atrium</u>





### Clinical features




* Most patients are asymptomatic.

* Less commonly: symptoms of <u>arrhythmias</u>, such as <u>palpitations</u>, <u>dizziness</u>, <u>syncope</u>, fatigue, and or <u>dyspnea</u>

* <u>Tachycardia</u>, often with a regular <u>pulse</u>

* Symptoms of the underlying disease (e.g., <u>murmurs</u> of <u>mitral stenosis</u>) may be present.





### Diagnostics [[18]](/library/sjbtbF)[[20]](/library/gx0FDR)[[68]](/library/Cmbq38)




* Similar to atrial fibrillation except for <u>ECG</u> findings (see “<u>Diagnosis of atrial fibrillation</u>”)

* Characteristic ECG findings of atrial flutter 

* Rate: typically 75–150/minute (depending on conduction)  [[68]](/library/Cmbq38)

* Atrial rate ≥ ventricular rate

* Narrow <u>QRS complexes</u>

* Characteristic rhythms

* Regular rhythm in <u>atrial flutter</u>: fixed AV conduction pattern (e.g., 2:1 or 4:1)

* <u>Regularly irregular rhythm</u> in <u>atrial flutter</u>: variable AV conduction and a consistent variation pattern (e.g., alternating between 2:1 and 3:1)

* <u>Irregularly irregular rhythm</u> in <u>atrial flutter</u>: variable AV conduction and an inconsistent variation pattern (i.e., no discernible pattern of AV conduction)

* Sawtooth appearance of P waves: identical <u>flutter waves</u> (F waves) that occur in sequence at a rate of ∼ 300/minute

* Predominantly negative deflections in leads II, III, <u>aVF</u>

* Flat deflections in I and aVL

### Treatment




Consult cardiology for all patients.




* Acute <u>management of rapid atrial flutter</u> is the same as the <u>management of Afib with RVR</u>.

* Long-term <u>arrhythmia</u> management is very similar to treatment of Afib with some minor differences:

* <u>Rate control</u>: more difficult to achieve in <u>atrial flutter</u> than in Afib [[18]](/library/sjbtbF)

* <u>Rhythm control</u>

* Better results and lower recurrence compared to Afib [[20]](/library/gx0FDR)[[68]](/library/Cmbq38)

* <u>Catheter ablation</u> may be the most effective <u>rhythm control strategy</u>.

* Anticoagulation recommendations are the same as for <u>long-term anticoagulation in Afib</u>.





### Complications




* Frequently degenerates into atrial fibrillation

* 1:1 conduction can lead to life-threatening <u>ventricular tachycardia</u>
